01.actor: Rav Aha bar Ya'akov (and the students of Rav Huna)
01.event: Rav Huna's long discourses left many of his students impotent; Rav Aha bar Ya'akov fell ill from holding back urine and was hung from the study hall's cedar column until a green substance came out of him.
01.turn: The cure worked and spared him the fate of the others.
01.outcome: He reported that of sixty elders, all became impotent except him, crediting the verse 'Wisdom preserves the life of him who has it.'
01.summary: Several sages, Rav Giddel, Rav Helbo and Rav Sheshet, became impotent from sitting through Rav Huna's long discourses. Rav Aha bar Ya'akov caught the illness that comes from holding back urine, so they hung him from the cedar column of the study hall, and a green substance came out of him and he was healed. He later said that of the sixty elders present, all became impotent except him, because he had used wisdom to preserve himself.

03.actor: a man testifying before Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
03.event: A man testified that someone had presumptive status as a Levite because he read second from the Torah.
03.turn: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi questioned whether the reading reflected Levite status or prominence, and the man answered that a priest had read before him.
03.outcome: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi elevated the person to Levite status on the man's word.
03.summary: A man came to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and said that someone he knew had established himself as a Levite. Asked what he had seen, he said the person was called second to the Torah in the synagogue. When the rabbi asked whether that might only reflect the person's prominence, the man explained that a priest had read just before him, so he was called as a Levite. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi then granted him Levite status on that testimony.

04.event: Absorbed in his learning, Nehemya walked beyond his Shabbat limit and could not return.
04.turn: Rav Hisda brought his student's distress to Rav Nahman.
04.outcome: Rav Nahman instructed that a human partition be formed so Nehemya could walk back in.
04.summary: Nehemya, son of Rav Hanilai, was so engrossed in study that he wandered outside his Shabbat boundary and was stuck. Rav Hisda told Rav Nahman that his student was in distress. Rav Nahman told him to have people line up as a human wall so Nehemya could walk back inside the boundary.
04.missing: The text does not state explicitly that the partition was formed and that he reentered.

05.event: Rabbi Zeira, who in Babylonia had believed the Rabbis disputed a ruling, went up to Eretz Yisrael and found Rabbi Asi teaching otherwise.
05.turn: He discovered that, per Rabbi Yohanan, all agree on the point and the dispute concerns a different formula.
05.summary: Rabbi Zeira recalled that in Babylonia they used to say the Rabbis disagreed with Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi about conditions phrased 'on the condition that.' When he went up to Eretz Yisrael, he found Rabbi Asi teaching in Rabbi Yohanan's name that everyone agrees on that point, and the dispute was only about 'from today and after death.'
05.missing: It is a report of a correction of a tradition; there is no further event or ending beyond the discovery.

06.event: Rava served drinks at his son's wedding; some sages stood for him and two, Rav Mari and Rav Pinehas, did not.
06.turn: The two who stayed seated failed to honor him.
06.outcome: Rava became angry and rebuked them, asking whether they alone were Sages and the others not.
06.summary: At his son's wedding Rava personally poured drinks for the guests. Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua stood up for him, but Rav Mari and Rav Pinehas son of Rav Hisda stayed seated. Rava grew angry and asked sarcastically whether those two were Sages and the ones who stood were not.

07.actor: a man who came to Rabbi Yosei
07.event: A man asked Rabbi Yosei whether a widow could perform halitza within three months of her husband's death.
07.turn: Told no, the man pushed back, asking what harm it would do.
07.outcome: Rabbi Yosei answered with a verse implying that only one eligible for levirate marriage may perform halitza.
07.summary: A man came to Rabbi Yosei and asked whether halitza could be performed within three months of the husband's death. Rabbi Yosei said it could not. The man challenged him, asking what would be wrong with it, and Rabbi Yosei cited the verse 'if the man does not wish to take her,' teaching that halitza applies only where levirate marriage would be possible.

08.event: Rabba issued a practical ruling about a bill of divorce found in a flax house in Pumbedita, following his own view.
08.outcome: He ruled according to his halakha; the circumstances are disputed.
08.summary: A bill of divorce was found in a flax house in Pumbedita, and Rabba ruled on it according to his own legal position. Traditions differ on the details: some say it was found where flax was soaked, a place caravans rarely pass, and others say where flax was sold, a busy place, but where no two men with the same name were known.
08.missing: The actual ruling (return or not) and any consequence are not narrated; the passage is mostly about the disputed circumstances.

09.actor: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and Rabbi Hiyya
09.event: When Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi fell ill, Rabbi Hiyya visited and found him crying.
09.turn: Rabbi Hiyya asked why he wept, since dying in tears is a bad omen.
09.outcome: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi explained that he was crying over the Torah and mitzvot he would no longer be able to fulfill.
09.summary: As Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi lay ill, Rabbi Hiyya came in and found him weeping. He asked his teacher why he was crying, reminding him of the teaching that dying while crying, or facing the wall, and the like, are bad signs. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi answered that he was weeping for the Torah and the commandments he would be unable to keep after death.

10.actor: Pishon the camel driver and his wife
10.event: Pishon's wife refused him (annulling the marriage) in his absence.
10.turn: The refusal was allowed because Pishon had mismanaged her property.
10.outcome: The Sages punished him measure for measure by validating the refusal.
10.summary: In a debate between Beit Hillel and Beit Shammai, the case of Pishon the camel driver comes up: his wife refused him while he was not present. Beit Shammai explained that because Pishon had dealt dishonestly with her property, the Sages dealt with him in the same defective measure and let the refusal stand.
10.missing: The incident is only cited as a precedent in an argument; how the refusal happened and its aftermath are not told.

11.actor: a woman holding a bag of documents
11.event: Heirs demanded a bag of documents deposited with a woman, who claimed she had seized it from the deceased while he was alive for a debt.
11.turn: Rav Nahman asked whether she had witnesses that the deceased demanded it in life and she refused, and she had none.
11.outcome: Rav Nahman ruled her seizure counted as after death and was worthless.
11.summary: A woman had a bag of documents deposited with her, and after the owner died his heirs came to claim it. She said she had taken it while he was still alive because he owed her money. Rav Nahman asked if she had witnesses that the man had asked for it back in his lifetime and she had refused; she did not. He therefore ruled that it was a seizure after death, which has no legal effect.

12.actor: a widow at Rabbi Yehuda's court
12.event: A woman came to testify before Rabbi Yehuda's court that her husband had died, and bystanders told her to lament, tear her clothes and loosen her hair.
12.turn: The coaching was meant to satisfy Rabbi Yehuda's requirement that she appear grieving.
12.summary: A woman came to Rabbi Yehuda's court to report her husband's death. People there told her to mourn openly, tear her clothes and unbind her hair so the court would believe her. They held she was permitted to remarry anyway, but wanted to make sure Rabbi Yehuda would also allow it.
12.missing: The outcome of her case is not given.

13.event: In a shepherds' village an inlet of the sea breached a courtyard wall, and the case came before Rav Yehuda.
13.outcome: Rav Yehuda required only one standing board to permit carrying there.
13.summary: Defending a ruling, Rav Yosef recalled a case in a shepherds' village where a narrow inlet of the sea broke through a courtyard wall. The question came to Rav Yehuda, who ruled that a single remaining board of wall was enough to permit carrying.
13.missing: Only a precedent cited in argument; no developed narrative beyond the ruling.

15.actor: the people of the Upper Galilee
15.event: The people of the Upper Galilee bought a litra of meat every day for a poor man of noble birth from Tzippori.
15.summary: The people of the Upper Galilee supported an impoverished man of noble background from Tzippori by buying him a litra of meat every day. The Gemara explains why this was remarkable: it was poultry, or it cost a fortune, or in such a small village an entire animal had to be slaughtered daily just for him.
15.missing: It describes an ongoing practice; there is no turn or ending.

16.event: Rav walked among the sheaves in a field and saw them waving in the wind.
16.outcome: He told them that business was still better than farming.
16.summary: Rav once went out among the standing grain and saw the stalks swaying. He addressed them, saying they could wave all they liked, but trade was more profitable than working the land.
16.missing: A brief anecdote framing a saying; no real turn.

17.actor: Levi, Ze'eiri and Rav Shimi bar Hiyya
17.event: On Shabbat, straw, fodder and water were brought to these sages through partitions formed by unwitting crowds.
17.summary: Like Rava's attendants, who once brought flasks into his house behind the crowd returning from his lecture, others used crowds as partitions: straw was brought in for Levi, fodder for Ze'eiri, and water for Rav Shimi bar Hiyya.
17.missing: Bare list of incidents with no turn or ending; the explanation of the method comes from the preceding context.

19.event: A student of Rabbi Eliezer was liable to death by burning for his sins.
19.turn: The Rabbis decided to spare him.
19.outcome: They let him alone because he had served a great man.
19.summary: Rabbi Eliezer had a student who had sinned so gravely that he deserved death by burning. The Rabbis said to leave him alone, because he had served a great person.
19.missing: What he did and what happened to him afterward are not told.

20.event: A man who had set his Shabbat-boundary eiruv with onions to reach Tiv'in came before Rabbi Meir in Ardiska.
20.turn: Rabbi Meir held that an onion eiruv is invalid, so the man was outside his limit.
20.outcome: Rabbi Meir confined him to his four cubits.
20.summary: Rabbi Meir was spending Shabbat in Ardiska when a man came to him and said he had made his boundary eiruv with onions so he could walk to Tiv'in. Rabbi Meir considered such an eiruv invalid, meaning the man had already passed his Shabbat limit. He ordered him to stay within his four cubits.
